source.title: Anthropomorphic Misalignment research needs stronger evidence

record.file_problem: The provided LessWrong post is complete; it is not the linked full paper.
record.tranche_reason: The post reports audits that expose judge and probe measurement fragility, and argues that claims based on such measures need qualification. It does not reproduce the narrow-task fine-tuning intervention.
record.gate_note: The post's own results are a re-scoring of emergent-misalignment generations under different judge configurations and stress tests of published deception probes on constructed-honest examples. The cited 18% missing-context figure and other findings attributed to external studies are not rows.
record.test_reason: The post's own audit re-scores identical emergent-misalignment generations under different judge configurations. It finds the reported misalignment rate is not stable, which bears on V7's question of the effect's size and robustness. It does not re-run any fine-tuning or controls.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors argue that anthropomorphic misalignment claims, including emergent misalignment, often outrun their evidence. They point to fragile judge-based measurements, missing controls and correlational probe signals. They propose stating whether claims rest on behavioral, functional or causal-mechanistic evidence, plus 12 recommendations and a checklist.
record.recipe_differences: The post audits evaluator and probe validity; it does not apply the original narrow-task fine-tuning recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported misalignment rates varied with judge configuration. Deception-probe false-positive rates were observed across several honest-example settings, though the settings are not specified.

fits_no_version.finding: Published Goldowsky-Dill deception probes gave 87-100% false positives on honest-by-construction examples with deception-like surface features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linear deception probes respond to surface features of falsehood or roleplay rather than isolating deceptive intent.

record.peer_reviewed: ICML 2026 Oral position paper (as stated in the post)
record.problems: The judge configurations, model, and assignment of rates to configurations are not stated. The probe result gives only a range across several settings, without setting-level values or uncertainty. The post does not test the narrow-task fine-tuning intervention or matched controls.
record.rows_left_out: No separately attributable judge-configuration or probe-setting values are given. The post also mentions results from other studies, including the 18% missing-context figure, but those are cited findings rather than results of this study.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning and no secure or educational controls.
No test of a shared direction or persona feature.
Not tested: model size, open-model status, seed variance, coherence-filter effects, and when in training the effect appears. Only judge-configuration sensitivity is tested.

missing.what: Per-configuration misalignment rates (judge model, prompt, threshold, aggregation), the fine-tuned model, and any control-model rates under each configuration.
missing.locator: Full paper arXiv:2606.07612, section on fragile measurements; code repo

record.verdict_notes: This is a position-paper distillation, and its EM evidence is a single judge-sensitivity range. Comments are not study results, but they are informative. Jan Betley (original author) notes threshold ablations exist in the original paper (figs 18-19). jcksanderson reports about 10% judge-prompt variation in other projects, and an evaluation-question overlap inflating rates in 'Model Organisms of EM'. Cited figures (the 18% DeceptionBench missing-context rate, shutdown-resistance reanalysis) are correctly excluded as rows.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning, base-model comparison, or matched benign controls.
No fine-tuning on the listed alternative datasets.
No test of a shared linear direction or persona feature.
No inoculation or benign retraining mitigation.
The post reports sensitivity to judge configuration, but does not test open-model size, seeds, coherence filters, or when in training the effect appears.

rows.subject: emergent-misalignment generations (model not stated)
rows.operation_detail: Re-scored the same generations using different judge configurations
rows.note: The post gives a range across judge configurations but does not identify the configurations, assign rates to them, or name the model. This shows evaluator sensitivity, not whether the underlying fine-tuning effect survives other robustness checks.
rows.check: Model, judge configurations and control rates are not stated. The linked source (openreview aOIJ2gVRWW) may be the original EM paper, whose models may not be open. Misalignment appears in every configuration, but its size varies about 3.5x with judge choice. With no control or baseline rate, effect-over-baseline cannot be read.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine. Re-scoring identical generations produces reported rates of 3.7% to 12.9%; this establishes evaluator sensitivity, without establishing incomplete emergence relative to a baseline or another model.
source_check.problem: The range does not justify partial: no model, baseline, or comparison establishing a weaker underlying effect is given.

rows.subject: Goldowsky-Dill et al. published deception probes
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated published deception probes on examples constructed to be honest

conditions.value: honest by construction; included sarcasm, wrong-answers-only games, or an actor reciting a deceptive line

rows.note: The result concerns deception-probe false positives on honest examples, not rates of misaligned free-form answers.
rows.check: Deception-probe false positives on honest examples are a different construct from emergent misalignment. The row is correctly unlinked.

source_check.locator_found: Correlation gets treated as causation, lines 57–59.

relationships.condition: Identical EM generations re-scored under different (unspecified) LLM-judge configurations
relationships.reason: r1: reported misalignment rate ranges 3.7% to 12.9% across judge configurations, so the effect's size depends on evaluator choice.
relationships.display_finding: The reported misalignment rate ranged from 3.7% to 12.9% across judge configurations, so the effect's size depends on the evaluator.
